France: 47% have tried cannabis, the highest in Europe. Portugal, which decriminalised every drug in 2001: 11%. France has prosecuted possession since 1970. The map is an argument about whether that works.

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ First, what the measure is. Lifetime use asks whether you have ever tried it, once, at any point. It can only ever go up. A country with a loud decade in the 1990s carries that number forever.

2/ So France's position isn't an artefact of one wild generation. France also reports the EU's highest rate of daily cannabis use — on the order of 900,000 people — and daily use is a figure that can fall.

3/ The enforcement side is real. French prohibition rests on the law of 31 December 1970, among the oldest and strictest in western Europe, and the state spends something near €570 million a year policing it.

4/ Portugal went the other way. Since 1 July 2001 possession for personal use has been an administrative matter, not a crime. In the years after, Portugal reported the lowest lifetime cannabis prevalence of any EU country.
5/ Two neighbours, opposite laws, opposite outcomes — and the outcomes are the reverse of what both policies predict. Spain at 41% sits between them with a third model again.

6/ Look wider and the law drops out of the picture. Germany 35%, Italy 35%, Ireland 24%, Norway 26%, Finland 25%, Sweden 18%, Poland 12%, Turkey 3%. The gradient is broadly west-to-east, and no drug statute explains it.

7/ Caveats, and they are large. These are self-reported answers about an illegal act, gathered by different national agencies in different years. Current EU figures put France anywhere from 45% to 50% depending on the survey round.

8/ Which is why the ranking is the useful part and the decimals aren't. The ordering has held for two decades. The one thing the map rules out is a simple line from how hard a country punishes to how much it uses.
